planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into fertile, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: This Chinese species daylily from Sichuan and Yunnan forms a neat, clump-forming rosette of arching, strap-shaped leaves well below the scale of modern hybrids. Slender scapes carry small, trumpet-shaped flowers in mid to golden yellow, each marked with an orange to golden throat. It tolerates heavier clay and poorer soils than many garden hybrids but flowers best with consistent moisture and full sun. Use it in a species collection, rock garden, or naturalized border where its smaller stature and early-season bloom add variety alongside larger-flowered daylily cultivars.

common_name: Flore Pleno Daylily (Historic Triple-Petaled Orange Species Daylily)

planting.note: Spreads by rhizomes; divide clumps every few years to control spread.

directions: Flore Pleno is a historic double-flowered selection of the common orange daylily, distinguished from the similar 'Kwanso' by a neater, more symmetrical arrangement of fifteen to eighteen recurved petals rather than the looser, muddled doubling of its better-known cousin. Like other fulva clones it is a vigorous, rhizomatous spreader that naturalizes readily and tolerates poor soil, drought, and neglect once established. The orange blooms carry faint red markings near the throat and open in mid to late summer above arching clumps of grassy foliage. Because it rarely sets seed, division is the only way to propagate true stock, and its spreading habit makes it best suited to naturalized areas or large masses rather than tidy borders.

common_name: Marion Vaughn Daylily (Historic Fragrant Lemon-Yellow Daylily)
directions: A mid-20th-century classic still widely grown, Marion Vaughn carries pale lemon-yellow, star-shaped flowers with a faint white midrib, opening wide in the evening and releasing a strong, sweet fragrance that carries well across a patio or border. Tall, well-branched scapes hold the blooms above narrow, arching foliage, blooming in mid to late season. Its vigor and clean color make it a dependable choice for massing or for scenting an evening garden, and it performs reliably in average garden soil with only routine watering and an occasional dividing of overcrowded clumps.

common_name: Mission Bells Daylily (Historic Soft Yellow Ruffled Daylily)
directions: One of the older soft-yellow daylily cultivars still in circulation, Mission Bells bears large, gently frilled flowers in a clear, warm yellow that holds its color well without fading in strong sun. Clumps form a well-shaped mound of arching foliage topped by sturdy scapes in mid-season. It is an easy, forgiving plant for an heirloom border or cottage-style planting, needing only average garden soil, full sun, and division every few years once clumps become crowded to keep bloom count high.

common_name: Pink Damask Daylily (Historic Deep Salmon-Pink Daylily)
directions: Pink Damask is a long-grown mid-century cultivar valued for deep salmon-pink, funnel-shaped flowers with a bright yellow throat and a subtle peach midrib on each petal. It blooms in mid-season with a tendency to send up a few later flushes, carried on tall, well-branched scapes above narrow arching foliage. Reliable and long-lived in the garden, it tolerates a wide range of soils and needs only full sun, routine moisture, and periodic division to stay vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Camden Gold Dollar Daylily (Compact Round Golden-Yellow Reblooming Daylily)
directions: Camden Gold Dollar produces small, nearly perfectly round, lightly ruffled flowers in bright golden yellow with a matching green throat, earning its coin-like common comparison. Compact scapes keep the floriferous blooms close to the semi-evergreen foliage, and the plant is notably free-flowering with a reliable late-season rebloom in many climates. Its short stature and tidy habit suit it to edging a border or massing along a walkway, and it asks for little beyond full sun, average watering, and occasional division once the clump thickens.

Dating from the earliest era of hybrid daylily breeding, Challenger carries classically shaped, medium ruddy brick-red flowers with a golden heart and creamy midribs, held on some of the tallest scapes of its generation. Good branching and bud count let it bloom well into late summer without staking despite its height, and the clump holds up reliably through wind and rain. It suits the back of a mixed border or a naturalized planting where its stature can be appreciated, and needs only full sun and routine garden care to perform for decades.

common_name: Star Over Oz Daylily (Fragrant Purple Crispate-Cascade Unusual-Form Daylily)
directions: Star Over Oz is a modern unusual-form cultivar whose large purple flowers carry twisted, pinched, and cascading petals around a bright star-shaped yellow eye, giving each bloom an exaggerated, sculptural look distinct from flat-form daylilies. The flowers are lightly fragrant and open on a well-branched, semi-evergreen plant that reblooms over the course of the season. Its dramatic, unusual petal form makes it a conversation-piece specimen for a border or collector's bed, and it grows under the same easy conditions as other modern diploid daylilies: full sun, average soil, and routine watering.

common_name: White Temptation Daylily (Classic Near-White Green-Throat Daylily)
directions: White Temptation is a long-standing favorite among near-white daylilies, with large, creamy-white self flowers set off by a vivid green throat that intensifies the sense of whiteness at a distance. Blooms open in the evening on a semi-evergreen plant with sturdy, well-branched scapes, and the flowers hold their form and color well in heat. It remains a benchmark for breeders working toward true white and is a reliable garden performer for a moon garden or pastel border, asking only for full sun and average watering.

common_name: Ming Porcelain Daylily (Fragrant Pastel Ivory-Pink and Gold Daylily)
directions: Ming Porcelain offers a delicate pastel blend of ivory and soft pink brushed with peach, edged in gold, and surrounded by a wide yellow halo over a lime-green throat, a subtle multi-tone effect reminiscent of antique porcelain glazes. The lightly fragrant, tetraploid blooms open on an evergreen plant with substantial, slightly ruffled petals. It pairs well with other pastel perennials in a soft-color border and performs reliably with full sun, average moisture, and the usual periodic division as clumps mature.

common_name: Little Fat Dazzler Daylily (Miniature Round Ruffled Fuchsia Daylily)
directions: True to its name, Little Fat Dazzler is a genuine miniature daylily standing barely a foot tall, yet its rounded, ruffled, bright fuchsia-rose flowers with a lemon-green throat are surprisingly large for so small a plant. Early to midseason blooms appear in abundance on a compact, semi-evergreen clump that stays tidy without crowding neighbors. Its small stature and oversized color impact make it an excellent choice for edging, rock gardens, or containers, and it needs only full sun and average watering to thrive.

Tiny Pumpkin carries small, bright golden-orange flowers just over two inches across with a green throat, held on scapes tall enough to show the blooms clearly above a compact, evergreen clump of grassy foliage. Flowering begins early to mid-season and continues over an extended period thanks to good bud count on a floriferous plant. Its diminutive flower size and cheerful color make it well suited to edging, mixed miniature-daylily collections, or small-space gardens, and it thrives in full sun with routine watering and occasional division.
